job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up late because I'm up till two coding. I share a rented room in a flat with two other people in Ashford Park, and my day starts with coffee and an AI assistant open next to my editor. I do job applications in the morning, maybe ten a day, then work on a side project and some small freelance gigs, like fixing a bakery's online ordering page. Evenings I'm on a Discord server with other graduates comparing rejections and swapping interview questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the job search, and where does it stand?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished a software engineering degree in June with a good result. My final project was a bus-timetable app that predicts delays, and I did a ten-week internship at a startup called Brightloop. When it ended, they said the funding was tight. Since then I've sent maybe 120 applications and got four interviews. Student debt is heavy, my savings would cover about three weeks, and my family can't help, so the freelance money is what pays my share of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means the tools are useful but they don't replace people. I'd tell the Discord group that employers are using hype as an excuse to freeze junior hiring either way. Hype or not, the market is bad for beginners and somebody should say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau means the market stays as bad as it is now. I use AI a lot, so I see where it helps and where it doesn't, and it won't change who gets hired. I'd still be one of two hundred people applying to every junior role, and with three weeks of savings that's a rough place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder on freelance work, because I can already get small paying jobs, and I'd try to turn two of them into regular monthly clients. I'd aim applications at smaller firms that use my stack, and offer a paid trial week to one or two of them. I'd also publish the bus-timetable app so it shows up when employers search my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. I'm not scared of tech, but I'm scared of running out of runway before anything turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a plateau, given you already use AI daily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding anyone who actually reads my application. I get automated rejections within an hour, which means nobody read it. Another hard part is the rent. If my freelance money dips, my flatmates notice, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the search right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn it into a small team thing. I know two other graduates who code well, and if we pooled our freelance contacts we could be a small agency. It's risky, but I'm comfortable with risk, and it's less risky than waiting for an email.

say: I'd say the tools help but employers use hype as an **excuse** to freeze junior hiring.
Somebody should say the market is bad for beginners.
think: A plateau keeps the market as bad as now, and I'd still be one of **two hundred** applicants.
Three weeks of savings is not much runway.
do: Push freelance work and turn two small clients into **monthly** ones.
Offer a paid trial week to small firms that use my stack.
Publish my bus-timetable app so employers find it when they search my name.
feel: **Restless**, not scared of tech but scared of running out of runway.
Uneasy that flatmates notice when freelance money dips.

fieldNote: He uses AI **daily**, so he judges its limits from experience, not headlines.
Freelance income is his bridge, and it makes him **practical** about risk.
Automated same-hour rejections hurt more than the lack of offers.

steps.text: Turn two freelance clients into monthly paying ones
Offer a paid trial week to small firms
Publish the bus-timetable app so employers can find it
Pitch two coder friends on a small freelance team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where graduates like me are lucky, because we grew up with the tools. I'd tell people to build things with AI, not just ask it questions. And I'd say firms and governments should fund retraining, because a lot of the people who write routine code are in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes my first job harder to land but my skills more useful once I'm in. A junior coder's first-year tasks are exactly what AI handles now: small features, bug fixes, tests, documentation. Firms ask, why hire three juniors when one person with good tools does it? I'm in the group that gets squeezed first, but also the group best placed to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell myself as a person who can ship fast with AI. I'd take on more freelance projects, charge slightly more, and aim for companies that are rewriting old systems. I'd also learn about testing and security, because someone has to check what the tools write. And I'd apply for roles that mix coding and talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped and nervous at once. I think this is the most exciting time to be coding, and the worst time to be a beginner with debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your freelance tasks does AI already do better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the boring stuff. Basic forms, simple scripts, CSS fixes. I used to spend a day on a bakery's order page. Now I do it in an hour, and the client doesn't think a day's worth of work is worth a day's price any more. So I'm quicker but I get paid for less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a graduate who refuses to use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not about liking it. It's like refusing to use a calculator in an accounts exam. You can, but the people next to you are faster. I'd also say use it with your eyes open, check everything, because it makes confident mistakes.

say: I'd tell people to **build** things with AI, not just ask it questions.
Governments should fund retraining for people who write routine code.
think: It makes my first job harder to land but my skills more **useful** once I'm in.

fieldNote: He sees the squeeze on juniors clearly yet counts on his **tool skills** as an edge.
Pricing is a real issue: clients pay for hours saved, not for what a day used to be worth.
Testing and security are his idea of **checking** work.

steps.text: Take on more freelance rewrites of old shop systems

Use AI tools to cut freelance delivery from a day to an hour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we should get ready, and not pretend it isn't. I'd push for basic income and retraining paid for by the companies who profit. Online, I'd call on everyone who codes to organise, because we're the first ones in the blast zone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's brutal. My whole field is the first one that's replaced. Two years from now an AI does what I do for pennies, and I'd still be paying a loan on a degree that taught me exactly that skill. I'm comfortable with risk, but this is more risk than I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop job hunting in software and start looking for anything that stays human the longest. I'd look into electrician or solar apprenticeships, where robots are about three years behind. In the meantime I'd keep taking freelance work, since I can earn cash fast now. I'd move out of my rented room to somewhere cheaper if it saves a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hard mix. Part of me is fascinated, because I'd be watching the biggest change in history, and the other part is terrified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do the day this is announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd text my flatmates and my parents, then book a call with someone who runs a trades apprenticeship. I'd ask what happens to the loan if I'm unemployed for years. And I'd try to work out how much I could earn in the next twenty-four months, because that is the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cash buffer. Right now it's three weeks, and I'd want three months of it. I'd sell my second monitor and my old console, and stop buying anything that isn't food or rent. Skills I can rebuild, a missed month of rent is harder to recover from.

say: I'd tell everyone who codes to **organise**, because we're the first ones in the blast zone.
Companies that profit should pay for retraining and basic income.
think: My field is the first replaced, and I'd still be paying a **loan** for it.
I'm comfortable with risk, but this is more than I can handle.
do: Look into electrician or solar **apprenticeships**, where robots are about three years behind.
Keep taking freelance work to earn cash fast.

feel: A hard mix of **fascination** and terror.
Watching the biggest change in history while it hits my own field.
S2.quote: I'm comfortable with risk, but this is more risk than I can handle.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** shows as a quick pivot toward trades the robots reach last.
He treats the two years as an earning window, to build a cash buffer.

steps.text: Ask a trades training provider about electrician apprenticeships
Build a three-month cash buffer by selling spare gear
Move to a cheaper room that saves a hundred monthly
Keep taking freelance work to earn cash quickly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for a plan, and I'd start laying out mine in public so others can copy or improve it. I'd write a post about how to use the time. I'd ask local colleges to run short AI-and-trades courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less afraid than in the 2028 world. I can get a first job, build a track record and then, if needed, pivot in year three or four. Software juniors will be hit hard, but someone who is good with AI tools and can also talk to clients should last a bit longer than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any software job that offers real mentoring, even at low pay, then save half of everything. I'd study a second skill on the side, probably electrical or energy systems, where the first robots will take longer. I'd also keep freelancing in case a full-time job falls through. By year three, I'd decide whether to stay or retrain fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the 2028 one. I'm still jumpy, but it feels like a race I can enter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change whether you'd stay in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Staying in software feels a bit like staying in a fire station when you know it's going to burn, but if I'm using the fire as it burns, I could build something. I'd stay at first and keep the exit route open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your three flatmates do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Jonas is a nurse and would be fine for the robots part. Priya works in marketing and is already worried. We'd probably sit down and compare plans, and I'd push us to share a rent that doesn't kill us.

say: I'd write a **public** post about how to use five years and ask colleges to run AI-and-trades courses.
think: I'm less afraid than in the 2028 world, since I can build a **track record** first.
People good with AI tools and clients should last a bit longer.

Save half of every pay cheque for a runway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're lucky to have this much time, and we should use it well. I'd tell friends to build things and not wait for permission. And I'd say the big firms should be told to fund retraining now, while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is plenty of time for me. I'd get a first job, learn a lot, maybe start a small company with friends, and be well on my way when it lands. I'd still worry about the rest of my generation, but I'd have time to get my own footing. The question is whether I'd have the discipline to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, pay the loan down aggressively, and use AI to build a couple of side products that bring in a little money. I'd also learn a trade-adjacent skill, like robotics maintenance, since someone has to look after the machines. I'd rent my own place within three years and save into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It feels like standing at the bottom of a hill that I can actually climb, and I'm good with hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, and I'd start a small business sooner. If I have ten years, my first year's loss or failure isn't fatal. In the 2028 world, a failed experiment is a disaster. With ten years, it's a lesson, and I like lessons that cost less than a month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your younger cousins to study computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say study computing, but also study how businesses work, how people talk to each other and how things are built. Coding alone is going to be a commodity. People who can talk to customers and spot problems stay valuable longer.

say: I'd tell friends to **build** things and not wait for permission.
Big firms should fund retraining now, while they can.
think: Ten years is plenty of time for a first job, a **small company** and a solid footing.
The only question is whether I'd have the discipline.

Comfortable with hills, less with debt.
S4.quote: In the 2028 world, a failed experiment is a disaster. With ten years, it's a lesson, and I like lessons that cost less than a month's rent.

steps.text: Pay the student loan down hard after the first job
Build two small AI-assisted side products for income
Learn robotics maintenance to look after machines
Put savings into a low-cost index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it kills all my options at the same time. In the longer ones I can experiment, take risks and recover. What would help is practical: paid trial jobs, someone who actually reads graduate applications, and a way to defer loan payments if there's no work. And fast, cheap training in trades for people like me who suddenly need a different route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with AI isn't a safe place. It makes me quick, but it also makes the work cheaper and my clients know it. I want people to know that using the tools is the minimum, not a magic pass. The real question is what we do when everyone is as fast as I am.

headlineQuote: Using the tools is the minimum, not a magic pass. The real question is what we do when everyone is as fast as I am.
portrait: Hassan is a **23-year-old** software engineering graduate sharing a rented room, with 120 applications, four interviews and no job offer.
He uses AI daily, freelances for small shops, and has about **three weeks** of savings against heavy student debt.
He leans progressive, wants retraining funded by firms and loan deferral, and organises with other graduates online.
Comfortable with risk, he pivots early, toward trades, side products and a possible **small** team.
Anxious in most pictures and alarmed with two years, he sees ten years as time to experiment.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because it removes all his options at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **trial** jobs, deferred loan payments when there's no work, and fast, cheap trades training.
